screens.narratorSegment: Responsive UI in Unity means designing interfaces that adapt to many screen sizes without manual repositioning. In this chapter you will learn the key components that automate layout and sizing: Layout Groups for structured arrangement, Content Size Fitter for content-driven sizing, Aspect Ratio Fitter for preserving proportions, and anchors and pivots for parent-relative behavior. These tools let your UI scale, reflow, and remain readable whether the game runs on a phone, tablet, or wide monitor. You will also see common pitfalls: conflicting fitters or using fixed pixel values that break responsiveness, and practical strategies to avoid them, like using layout elements and minimizing nested groups. Finally, there is a hands-on inventory panel workflow that combines a vertical category list and a grid of square item slots, showing how these pieces come together in a real interface. By the end of the chapter you’ll understand not just what each component does, but how to combine them to build robust, performant, and flexible UI. Think about a menu that must remain usable when the game window is resized — that real need is why these tools matter.

screens.title: Layout Groups — What they are and when to use them
screens.narratorSegment: Layout Groups are components that automatically position and size child UI elements based on rules you set, so you avoid manual placement for every resolution. A Horizontal Layout Group lines up children side by side and is ideal for toolbars or rows of buttons. A Vertical Layout Group stacks children top to bottom, great for menus or lists. The Grid Layout Group arranges children into rows and columns with configurable cell size and spacing, perfect for inventories or icon collections. A clear example: a toolbar of action buttons should use a Horizontal Layout Group so adding a new button updates spacing automatically. A common misconception is thinking you can freely manually move children inside a Layout Group; instead, the group overrides child Rect Transforms. The right workflow is to adjust the Layout Group settings—padding, spacing, child alignment—or add a Layout Element to the child to give min or preferred sizes. Performance tip: avoid excessive nested groups when many children are present because each group adds layout calculations. Quick test: create a parent, add a Vertical Layout Group, drop a few button children, then change spacing and see how children reposition without manual edits. That validation will help you trust groups rather than manual coordinates. Where might you still use manual layout? For highly custom or animated arrangements, but even then you can combine animation with groups by animating the group parameters, not the child transforms directly. What is one thing you will check first when a layout seems broken? Verify whether a Layout Group is present and if child positions were edited manually — if they were, revert to group settings or use Layout Element to influence size.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.5 › Layout Groups
Definition

Layout Groups are Unity components that automatically arrange and optionally control size of their child Rect Transforms, reducing manual layout work across varying screen sizes.

Horizontal Layout Group
Best for toolbars and rows. Children are placed left-to-right and spacing/padding controls gaps.
Vertical Layout Group
Best for lists and menus. Children stack top-to-bottom and can force expand or preserve sizes.
Grid Layout Group
Arranges children into cells with configurable cell size, spacing, and constraints for columns or rows.
Common mistake
Manually moving children inside a Layout Group will be overridden. Use Layout Element to influence a child's size.
Pro tip
Adjust padding and spacing on the Layout Group or add Layout Elements to children for min/preferred sizes.
Visual examples (simulated)
Toolbar (Horizontal)
A
B
C
Category list (Vertical)
Weapons
Armor
Consumables
Inventory grid (Grid)
Key Takeaway

Choose the Layout Group that matches the structure you need and control child sizing via Layout Elements rather than manual transforms.

screens.title: Using Horizontal & Vertical Layout Groups
screens.narratorSegment: Setting up a horizontal toolbar or a vertical category list is a common task that benefits from a clear sequence. First, create a parent GameObject and add the appropriate Layout Group component: Horizontal for toolbars, Vertical for lists. Second, configure padding and spacing so the children have adequate separation. Third, decide whether children should have flexible widths or fixed sizes — enable Child Force Expand when you want even distribution, or leave it off and set child Layout Element preferred sizes for precise control. Fourth, add children (buttons, icons) as regular UI objects and avoid manually moving them; the group determines their position. A concrete example: make a Horizontal Layout Group for an ability bar. Add five button children and set spacing to eight. If you want the middle button to be wider, add a Layout Element to it and increase preferred width — the group will respect that element when configured. A misconception to avoid is toggling both Child Force Expand and giving large preferred widths to many children; these settings can contradict and produce unexpected sizing. For verification, resize the Game view and watch the toolbar or list respond. If you see clipping or overlapping, check whether the parent anchor or Rect Transform is constrained incorrectly or whether nested layout groups are adding complexity. Finally, prefer minimal nesting: combine alignment and spacing in one group where possible, and only add nested groups for distinct regions of behavior.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.5 › Horizontal & Vertical Groups
Step-by-step
  1. Add parent GameObject and the Layout Group component that matches the layout need.
  2. Adjust padding and spacing to set the visual rhythm and avoid crowding.
  3. Decide on Child Force Expand or per-child Layout Elements for size control.
  4. Drop children into the parent and avoid manual repositioning; use Layout Element to change a child's width or height when necessary.
  5. Validate by resizing the Game view and looking for clipping or overlap.
Example
A five-button ability bar uses a Horizontal Layout Group with spacing 8. Make a central button wider by adding a Layout Element and increasing preferred width.
Visual checks
Child Force Expand: ON
Children share available space evenly. Use when you want uniform elements.
Child Force Expand: OFF + Layout Element
Give selected children preferred sizes for precise control while others remain flexible.
Common Mistake
Manually setting child positions then using a Layout Group — the group will override your manual placement.
Key Takeaway

Decide whether to give all children equal space or specialized sizes, then configure the group accordingly.

screens.title: Content Size Fitter — Size to content safely
screens.narratorSegment: The Content Size Fitter controls a Rect Transform so it grows or shrinks to match its child's measured content size. There are two axes to consider: Horizontal Fit and Vertical Fit, each of which can be Unconstrained, Min Size, or Preferred Size. Unconstrained makes the fitter inactive on that axis. Min Size guarantees at least the content size but allows expansion, while Preferred Size forces the element to match the content's preferred dimensions. A practical situation is a dialog with variable text: set Vertical Fit to Preferred Size on the Text object so the background panel can use a Layout Group or parent resizing to accommodate the larger text length. A typical misconception is applying a Content Size Fitter to a child inside a Layout Group without considering the parent — the fitter may attempt to expand and collide with the group's sizing rules. When that happens, add a Layout Element to the child or change the group's control child width/height settings. Another caution: ensure the parent has room to expand, or the child may overflow beyond bounds. For performance and predictability, avoid arbitrary chains of fitters that cause repeated layout recalculations. Instead, use fitters for content-driven elements and let Layout Groups manage alignment.

keyIdea.text: Use Content Size Fitter to let UI elements expand to fit text or images, but coordinate with parent layout to prevent conflicts.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.5 › Content Size Fitter
How it works

Content Size Fitter measures a content component (like TextMeshProUGUI) and sets the Rect Transform size to match either the minimum or preferred content size depending on your settings.

Fit Modes
  • Unconstrained — no automatic sizing
  • Min Size — ensures at least content size
  • Preferred Size — match content preferred size
Example
A description text set to Vertical Fit: Preferred Size expands the text box vertically to contain long paragraphs, avoiding clipping without manual height adjustments.
Warnings & tips
Conflict example
A Content Size Fitter on a child inside a Horizontal Layout Group may fight with the group's control child width setting. Resolve by using a Layout Element or disabling control width on the group.
Parent space
Ensure parent Rect Transform can expand. Otherwise the child may overflow outside visible bounds.
Performance
Limit cascading fitters and nested recalculations to avoid costly layout passes each frame.
Key Takeaway

Use Content Size Fitter where content length varies, and coordinate with parent layout rules to avoid conflicts and overflow.

screens.title: Aspect Ratio Fitter — Preserve proportions
screens.narratorSegment: Aspect Ratio Fitter makes a UI element maintain a fixed width-to-height ratio regardless of the parent size. It offers modes like FitInParent, EnvelopeParent, WidthControlsHeight, and HeightControlsWidth, and you set the numeric ratio, for example 1 for square or 1.777 for 16:9. A common use case is inventory item slots that must remain square even when their grid cell size changes. To implement this, set each slot's Aspect Ratio Fitter to WidthControlsHeight and an Aspect Ratio of 1. This ensures the width determines the height and keeps a perfect square. A frequent misconception is expecting an Aspect Ratio Fitter to work without considering the Layout Group controlling cell size; the fitter sets the child's Rect Transform based on the selected mode, but the parent grid cell or the group's cell size can still influence the result. When combining with Grid Layout Group, choose a Grid cell size that provides the desired width; the Aspect Ratio Fitter will compute height accordingly when set to WidthControlsHeight. Also beware of EnvelopeParent mode when the parent has an unusual shape; test across multiple aspect ratios. The takeaway: use Aspect Ratio Fitter to guarantee visual consistency for assets that must not distort.

keyIdea.text: Use Aspect Ratio Fitter modes and a numeric ratio to stop images and slots from stretching across different resolutions.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.5 › Aspect Ratio Fitter
What it controls

Aspect Ratio Fitter enforces a numerical width-to-height ratio and offers different modes for how the child relates to the parent or its own width/height.

Modes
  • FitInParent — scale to fit inside parent
  • EnvelopeParent — cover parent, may overflow
  • WidthControlsHeight — compute height from width
  • HeightControlsWidth — compute width from height
Example
Item slot: set WidthControlsHeight with Aspect Ratio 1 so width determines height and each slot stays square when the grid cell size changes.
Integration tips
With Grid Layout Group
Set cell size to a target width; use WidthControlsHeight so height follows and slots remain proportional to the cell width.
Common Mistake
Assuming the fitter overrides parent sizing—if the parent cell size is constrained, adjust the parent or use a different mode.
Validation
Resize the Game view and ensure images or slots do not distort or clip; adjust mode if necessary.
Key Takeaway

Use Aspect Ratio Fitter to guarantee assets remain undistorted, and choose the mode that matches parent constraints.

screens.title: Anchors and Pivots — Parent-relative positioning
screens.narratorSegment: Anchors and pivots determine how a Rect Transform behaves relative to its parent. Anchors are reference points inside the parent rectangle. Common anchor presets include stretch-stretch to make a background fill its parent, stretch-top to create a header that stretches its width, or fixed anchors for elements that should stay a constant distance from a corner. Pivots define the local origin of an element — where scaling and rotation are applied from. A practical consequence is how health bars scale: if you want a bar to shrink from right to left, set the pivot to the right edge so scaling reduces width toward the left. Anchors control position and relative sizing; pivots control transformation origin. An important misconception is thinking anchors and pivots are interchangeable; they serve different purposes and both must be set correctly for responsive behavior. For instance, a footer should typically have stretch-bottom anchors and a central pivot, whereas a tooltip that grows from its top-left corner should have anchors locked and a pivot at top-left. Always test by resizing the Game view: anchors will dictate whether an element stretches with the parent or maintains offsets. When using Layout Groups, anchors are often set to stretch to allow the group to compute child sizes, but specific children may require custom pivots for animation effects. The final check: does the element keep its intended relative position and animation origin across aspect ratios? If not, revisit anchors and pivots.

keyIdea.text: Anchors set parent-relative reference and stretch behavior; pivots define the local origin for scaling and rotation.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.5 › Anchors & Pivots
Anchors

Anchors define how a child is positioned relative to its parent rect. Use stretch anchors for backgrounds and top/bottom presets for headers or footers.

Stretch example
Background Image uses stretch-stretch anchors so it always fills the parent canvas or panel.
Header example
Header uses stretch-top anchors, fixed height, and stretches across the width regardless of aspect ratio.
Pivots

Pivots define the local origin for running transforms. Set a pivot to the right for bars that should shrink from right to left or to the left for the opposite behavior.

Health bar example
Set pivot X to 1 (right edge) so scaling the width appears to empty the bar toward the left rather than shifting its origin.
Tooltip example
A tooltip that grows downward uses a top-left pivot so the top-left corner remains fixed as the box expands.
Key Takeaway

Set anchors to control stretch and offsets; set pivots to control animation and scaling origins. Both must be checked when responsive behavior breaks.

screens.title: Common conflicts and how to resolve them
screens.narratorSegment: Conflicts arise when multiple systems try to control the same Rect Transform. A frequent case is placing a Content Size Fitter on a child inside a Layout Group that also controls child width or height. The conflict causes oscillation or unexpected sizes because the fitter tries to set the size while the group overrides it. The solution is to pick one authority for each axis: either let the group control size and use Layout Element constraints for the child, or disable control on the group and allow the fitter to size the child. Another issue is deep nesting of Layout Groups. Each nested group requires additional layout passes and can degrade performance, especially with many children. Simplify structure: use fewer groups, consolidate spacing at higher levels, or batch dynamically-created children under a single group when possible. Avoid hard-coded pixel sizes for position and size where responsiveness is needed. Fixed pixels may look correct on your desktop but break on other aspect ratios. Instead, use anchors, percent-relative sizing through stretch anchors, or flexible Layout Group options. A concrete example: if a text description grows and pushes other content, ensure the parent is allowed to expand or place the description in a scrollable area. Ask yourself: which component should be the single source of truth for each dimension? That choice reduces conflicts and makes behavior predictable.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.5 › Conflicts & Performance
Common Conflicts
  • Content Size Fitter on a child inside a Layout Group trying to control the same axis.
  • Nested Layout Groups causing repeated layout calculations and lag.
  • Fixed pixel sizes that prevent elements from reflowing across aspect ratios.
Resolution pattern
Decide which component owns each axis, simplify group nesting, use Layout Element to expose child sizing preferences, and validate by resizing the Game view.
Performance tips
Minimize nested groups
Flatten the structure where possible. Group related items under a single Layout Group instead of multiple levels.
Batch updates
When adding many children at runtime, disable layout rebuilds, add children, then re-enable to avoid repeated recalculations.
Validation
Use the profiler and test with many children to detect layout costs early.
Common Mistake

Applying both the Layout Group and a Content Size Fitter to the same axis without a clear owner causes unpredictable sizing or layout thrashing.

screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on workflow ties the chapter concepts together. Start by creating an InventoryPanel parent with anchors set to middle-center and an initial size, then add a CategoriesContainer on the left with a Vertical Layout Group. On the right, create ItemGridContainer and attach a Grid Layout Group with a fixed column count and cell size. For each ItemSlot child, add an Image and an Aspect Ratio Fitter set to WidthControlsHeight with a ratio of 1 to keep slots square. Duplicate slots to fill a typical inventory. Module 04 › Chapter 4.5 › Inventory Workflow
Step-by-step Build
  1. Create InventoryPanel parent and set anchors to middle-center.
  2. Add CategoriesContainer on the left; attach Vertical Layout Group with padding and spacing, enable Child Force Expand Width.
  3. Add ItemGridContainer on the right; attach Grid Layout Group with fixed column count and chosen cell size.
  4. Create ItemSlot with Image + Aspect Ratio Fitter (WidthControlsHeight, ratio 1) and duplicate into grid cells.
  5. Add ItemDescription text with Content Size Fitter (Vertical Fit: Preferred Size) so the background grows with text.
Validation Checklist
  • Resize Game view and confirm layout reflows.
  • Paste long description and confirm expansion without clipping.
  • Ensure item slots remain square when cell size changes.
Common fixes
Fix: Content Size Fitter conflict
If a child fitter conflicts with grid sizing, use a Layout Element or move the content into an unconstrained area.
Fix: Pixel offsets
Replace hard-coded offsets with anchor presets and relative offsets so the panel adapts to different aspect ratios.
Key Takeaway

Combine layout groups and fitters with clear ownership per axis, then validate by resizing and adding dynamic content.

screens.title: Common assessment scenarios
screens.narratorSegment: When a UI element behaves unexpectedly after resizing, follow a short diagnosis routine. First, identify which component is trying to control the problematic axis: is it a Layout Group, a Content Size Fitter, an Aspect Ratio Fitter, or a manually set Rect Transform? Second, inspect the parent: are its anchors and pivot set to allow the desired behavior, or is the parent constraining children? Third, check for Layout Elements on the child that may set min or preferred sizes. Fourth, test turning off control flags on the Layout Group (for example, disable Control Child Width) to see if the fitter regains control or vice versa. A practical assessment question from the chapter asks how to build a 3x3 square equipment grid: the correct solution uses a Grid Layout Group with Fixed Column Count set to 3 and Aspect Ratio Fitter on each slot with WidthControlsHeight and a ratio of 1. Another assessment checks Content Size Fitter usage: to let a TextMeshPro element expand vertically, add the Content Size Fitter and set Vertical Fit to Preferred Size. These checks are rapid and reproducible — they let you find the single owner of an axis and fix conflicts by assigning a single source of truth for that axis. When you practice this routine, debugging layout issues becomes quick and predictable.

Diagnosis Steps

screens.title: Performance & maintainability tips
screens.narratorSegment: Maintaining responsive UI at scale requires attention to both performance and maintainability. First, limit deep nesting of Layout Groups — each group causes a layout rebuild when children change. When adding or removing many children at runtime, batch the operation: disable layout rebuilds, perform the changes, and re-enable rebuilds to force a single layout pass. Second, prefer simple structures: group children logically and avoid one-off nested groups unless necessary. Third, use Layout Element to capture size rules at the child level rather than many separate configuration scripts. Fourth, document layout ownership: note which component controls each axis and any Layout Elements that set preferred sizes. This is especially useful for teams or when revisiting a scene later. Fifth, keep anchors and pivots consistent across similar elements so animations and scaling behave predictably. Lastly, test on multiple aspect ratios early. Small visual regressions compound as UI complexity grows, so catching them early saves time. A short checklist: reduce nesting, batch updates, document ownership, and run resize tests. These practices keep UI responsive and performant while making later changes safer. In practical terms, minimize layout overhead and design for future changes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. fullNarratorScript:
Responsive UI in Unity means designing interfaces that adapt to many screen sizes without manual repositioning. In this chapter you will learn the key components that automate layout and sizing: Layout Groups for structured arrangement, Content Size Fitter for content-driven sizing, Aspect Ratio Fitter for preserving proportions, and anchors and pivots for parent-relative behavior. These tools let your UI scale, reflow, and remain readable whether the game runs on a phone, tablet, or wide monitor. You will also see common pitfalls: conflicting fitters or using fixed pixel values that break responsiveness, and practical strategies to avoid them, like using layout elements and minimizing nested groups. Finally, there is a hands-on inventory panel workflow that combines a vertical category list and a grid of square item slots, showing how these pieces come together in a real interface. By the end of the chapter you’ll understand not just what each component does, but how to combine them to build robust, performant, and flexible UI. Think about a menu that must remain usable when the game window is resized — that real need is why these tools matter.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to arrange UI elements automatically with Layout Groups, ensure UI elements resize to fit content with the Content Size Fitter, preserve visual proportions with the Aspect Ratio Fitter, and control how elements react to screen changes using anchors and pivots. First, you will learn to pick the right Layout Group for a task: horizontal for toolbars, vertical for lists, and grid for item slots. Second, you will practice using Content Size Fitter to stop text clipping and let backgrounds expand when content changes. Third, you will apply Aspect Ratio Fitter to keep portraits and icons from stretching. Fourth, you will master anchors and pivots so elements stretch or maintain position relative to their parent. Each objective includes a practical milestone that verifies competency, such as building an inventory UI that remains usable when the Game view is resized. These are hands-on skills: the goal is not only to understand each component but to combine them correctly without conflicts. Keep an eye out for common mistakes like setting fixed pixel sizes or nesting many layout groups, and learn why those patterns can break responsiveness.

This second objectives slide focuses on real outcomes and small checks you can use while building. You will implement a Vertical Layout Group to create category lists where buttons expand consistently, and a Grid Layout Group to arrange square item slots. You will configure a Content Size Fitter on a description text so the background panel grows as text gets longer, and you will attach an Aspect Ratio Fitter to item slots to keep them square even when the grid cell size changes. You will also demonstrate anchors and pivots by making a header that stretches horizontally and a health bar that scales from right to left using a pivot on the right edge. For each outcome, a short verification step is provided: resize the Game view and check for clipping, distortion, or misalignment. These are simple, repeatable tests that prove your setup is responsive and robust. Practicing these checks saves time later and reduces platform-specific bugs.

Layout Groups are components that automatically position and size child UI elements based on rules you set, so you avoid manual placement for every resolution. A Horizontal Layout Group lines up children side by side and is ideal for toolbars or rows of buttons. A Vertical Layout Group stacks children top to bottom, great for menus or lists. The Grid Layout Group arranges children into rows and columns with configurable cell size and spacing, perfect for inventories or icon collections. A clear example: a toolbar of action buttons should use a Horizontal Layout Group so adding a new button updates spacing automatically. A common misconception is thinking you can freely manually move children inside a Layout Group; instead, the group overrides child Rect Transforms. The right workflow is to adjust the Layout Group settings—padding, spacing, child alignment—or add a Layout Element to the child to give min or preferred sizes. Performance tip: avoid excessive nested groups when many children are present because each group adds layout calculations. Quick test: create a parent, add a Vertical Layout Group, drop a few button children, then change spacing and see how children reposition without manual edits. That validation will help you trust groups rather than manual coordinates. Where might you still use manual layout? For highly custom or animated arrangements, but even then you can combine animation with groups by animating the group parameters, not the child transforms directly. What is one thing you will check first when a layout seems broken? Verify whether a Layout Group is present and if child positions were edited manually — if they were, revert to group settings or use Layout Element to influence size.

Setting up a horizontal toolbar or a vertical category list is a common task that benefits from a clear sequence. First, create a parent GameObject and add the appropriate Layout Group component: Horizontal for toolbars, Vertical for lists. Second, configure padding and spacing so the children have adequate separation. Third, decide whether children should have flexible widths or fixed sizes — enable Child Force Expand when you want even distribution, or leave it off and set child Layout Element preferred sizes for precise control. Fourth, add children (buttons, icons) as regular UI objects and avoid manually moving them; the group determines their position. A concrete example: make a Horizontal Layout Group for an ability bar. Add five button children and set spacing to eight. If you want the middle button to be wider, add a Layout Element to it and increase preferred width — the group will respect that element when configured. A misconception to avoid is toggling both Child Force Expand and giving large preferred widths to many children; these settings can contradict and produce unexpected sizing. For verification, resize the Game view and watch the toolbar or list respond. If you see clipping or overlapping, check whether the parent anchor or Rect Transform is constrained incorrectly or whether nested layout groups are adding complexity. Finally, prefer minimal nesting: combine alignment and spacing in one group where possible, and only add nested groups for distinct regions of behavior.

The Content Size Fitter controls a Rect Transform so it grows or shrinks to match its child's measured content size. There are two axes to consider: Horizontal Fit and Vertical Fit, each of which can be Unconstrained, Min Size, or Preferred Size. Unconstrained makes the fitter inactive on that axis. Min Size guarantees at least the content size but allows expansion, while Preferred Size forces the element to match the content's preferred dimensions. A practical situation is a dialog with variable text: set Vertical Fit to Preferred Size on the Text object so the background panel can use a Layout Group or parent resizing to accommodate the larger text length. A typical misconception is applying a Content Size Fitter to a child inside a Layout Group without considering the parent — the fitter may attempt to expand and collide with the group's sizing rules. When that happens, add a Layout Element to the child or change the group's control child width/height settings. Another caution: ensure the parent has room to expand, or the child may overflow beyond bounds. For performance and predictability, avoid arbitrary chains of fitters that cause repeated layout recalculations. Instead, use fitters for content-driven elements and let Layout Groups manage alignment.

Aspect Ratio Fitter makes a UI element maintain a fixed width-to-height ratio regardless of the parent size. It offers modes like FitInParent, EnvelopeParent, WidthControlsHeight, and HeightControlsWidth, and you set the numeric ratio, for example 1 for square or 1.777 for 16:9. A common use case is inventory item slots that must remain square even when their grid cell size changes. To implement this, set each slot's Aspect Ratio Fitter to WidthControlsHeight and an Aspect Ratio of 1. This ensures the width determines the height and keeps a perfect square. A frequent misconception is expecting an Aspect Ratio Fitter to work without considering the Layout Group controlling cell size; the fitter sets the child's Rect Transform based on the selected mode, but the parent grid cell or the group's cell size can still influence the result. When combining with Grid Layout Group, choose a Grid cell size that provides the desired width; the Aspect Ratio Fitter will compute height accordingly when set to WidthControlsHeight. Also beware of EnvelopeParent mode when the parent has an unusual shape; test across multiple aspect ratios. The takeaway: use Aspect Ratio Fitter to guarantee visual consistency for assets that must not distort.

Anchors and pivots determine how a Rect Transform behaves relative to its parent. Anchors are reference points inside the parent rectangle. Common anchor presets include stretch-stretch to make a background fill its parent, stretch-top to create a header that stretches its width, or fixed anchors for elements that should stay a constant distance from a corner. Pivots define the local origin of an element — where scaling and rotation are applied from. A practical consequence is how health bars scale: if you want a bar to shrink from right to left, set the pivot to the right edge so scaling reduces width toward the left. Anchors control position and relative sizing; pivots control transformation origin. An important misconception is thinking anchors and pivots are interchangeable; they serve different purposes and both must be set correctly for responsive behavior. For instance, a footer should typically have stretch-bottom anchors and a central pivot, whereas a tooltip that grows from its top-left corner should have anchors locked and a pivot at top-left. Always test by resizing the Game view: anchors will dictate whether an element stretches with the parent or maintains offsets. When using Layout Groups, anchors are often set to stretch to allow the group to compute child sizes, but specific children may require custom pivots for animation effects. The final check: does the element keep its intended relative position and animation origin across aspect ratios? If not, revisit anchors and pivots.

Conflicts arise when multiple systems try to control the same Rect Transform. A frequent case is placing a Content Size Fitter on a child inside a Layout Group that also controls child width or height. The conflict causes oscillation or unexpected sizes because the fitter tries to set the size while the group overrides it. The solution is to pick one authority for each axis: either let the group control size and use Layout Element constraints for the child, or disable control on the group and allow the fitter to size the child. Another issue is deep nesting of Layout Groups. Each nested group requires additional layout passes and can degrade performance, especially with many children. Simplify structure: use fewer groups, consolidate spacing at higher levels, or batch dynamically-created children under a single group when possible. Avoid hard-coded pixel sizes for position and size where responsiveness is needed. Fixed pixels may look correct on your desktop but break on other aspect ratios. Instead, use anchors, percent-relative sizing through stretch anchors, or flexible Layout Group options. A concrete example: if a text description grows and pushes other content, ensure the parent is allowed to expand or place the description in a scrollable area. Ask yourself: which component should be the single source of truth for each dimension? That choice reduces conflicts and makes behavior predictable.

This hands-on workflow ties the chapter concepts together. Start by creating an InventoryPanel parent with anchors set to middle-center and an initial size, then add a CategoriesContainer on the left with a Vertical Layout Group. Configure padding and enable Child Force Expand Width so category buttons fill the left column. On the right, create ItemGridContainer and attach a Grid Layout Group with a fixed column count and cell size. For each ItemSlot child, add an Image and an Aspect Ratio Fitter set to WidthControlsHeight with a ratio of 1 to keep slots square. Duplicate slots to fill a typical inventory. Next, create an ItemDescription text object and add a Content Size Fitter with Vertical Fit set to Preferred Size so descriptions grow without clipping. If conflicts occur, either set the Grid to control cell size and let the fitter only determine the content height, or move the description out of the constrained grid area. This workflow demonstrates how Layout Groups, Fitters, and Anchors must be coordinated to build a resilient interface.

When a UI element behaves unexpectedly after resizing, follow a short diagnosis routine. First, identify which component is trying to control the problematic axis: is it a Layout Group, a Content Size Fitter, an Aspect Ratio Fitter, or a manually set Rect Transform? Second, inspect the parent: are its anchors and pivot set to allow the desired behavior, or is the parent constraining children? Third, check for Layout Elements on the child that may set min or preferred sizes. Fourth, test turning off control flags on the Layout Group (for example, disable Control Child Width) to see if the fitter regains control or vice versa. These checks are rapid and reproducible — they let you find the single owner of an axis and fix conflicts by assigning a single source of truth for that axis. Maintaining responsive UI at scale requires attention to both performance and maintainability. First, limit deep nesting of Layout Groups — each group causes a layout rebuild when children change. When adding or removing many children at runtime, batch the operation: disable layout rebuilds, perform the changes, and re-enable rebuilds to force a single layout pass. Second, prefer simple structures: group children logically and avoid one-off nested groups unless necessary. Third, use Layout Element to capture size rules at the child level rather than many separate configuration scripts. Fourth, document layout ownership: note which component controls each axis and any Layout Elements that set preferred sizes. This is especially useful for teams or when revisiting a scene later. Fifth, keep anchors and pivots consistent across similar elements so animations and scaling behave predictably. Lastly, test on multiple aspect ratios early. Keep these three concise reminders handy as you work. First, Layout Groups are the go-to tool for consistent arrangement — use Horizontal, Vertical, or Grid depending on structure. Third, Anchors and Pivots control parent-relative behavior and animation origins; set them intentionally.
